label: When You Are Suffering
framing: Scripture does not explain your suffering away or hand you a reason that makes the wound smaller. It gives you a God who entered the pain himself, a Savior acquainted with grief, and the stubborn promise that nothing you suffer is wasted or unseen.
cultural: The book of Job was written into a world that assumed suffering was always punishment, that the afflicted had earned their affliction. Job's friends spoke the common wisdom of the ancient Near East, and God silenced it. Paul wrote of his thorn in the flesh to readers who knew beatings, shipwreck, and prison as ordinary costs of following Christ in the Roman world.
historical: The church has refused both the lie that suffering is meaningless and the lie that it is simply deserved. Augustine in the fifth century wrote of God bringing good out of evil rather than sparing us from it, and Martin Luther, in the sixteenth century, taught that God is found not on the heights but at the cross, hidden in the very suffering we would flee.
application: Do not let anyone, including yourself, shame you for hurting or rush you toward a tidy lesson. Bring the pain to God honestly, as Job did, and let trusted people carry part of the weight. Look for God in the suffering rather than only beyond it. If pain is crushing you to the point of despair, reach for a doctor, a counselor, or a pastor, and treat that as faith and not its failure.

verses.text: Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.
I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us.
Though He slay me, I will hope in Him. I will still defend my ways to His face.

related.label: Suffering and the Silence of God

label: When You Are Waiting on God
framing: Scripture takes waiting seriously, because it knows how long God's people have had to wait. It does not promise the wait will be short, but it promises that the God who seems slow is not absent, and that those who wait on him renew their strength.
cultural: Abraham waited twenty-five years for a son, Israel waited four hundred years in Egypt, and the prophets waited centuries for a Messiah who came only in the fullness of time. The biblical world measured God's faithfulness across generations, not days, and learned to hope against the evidence of the moment.
historical: The church has prayed Come, Lord Jesus for two thousand years and learned to call the wait Advent, a season of longing built into the calendar. The Psalms of waiting shaped monastic prayer from the start, and figures like John of the Cross, in the sixteenth century, wrote of the dark night when God seems silent yet is doing the deepest work.
application: Waiting is not wasted time, though it rarely feels otherwise. Keep praying the request honestly, even when heaven seems quiet, and let the wait do its slow work in you rather than only watching the clock. Tell the truth about how hard it is, and lean on people who have waited longer and not given up. Trust that the delay is not the same as denial.

verses.text: But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.
Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!
I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope. My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning— more than watchmen wait for the morning.
The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him. It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.
For the vision awaits an appointed time; it testifies of the end and does not lie. Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay.

label: When You Are Afraid
framing: Scripture says do not be afraid again and again, and it is never spoken to deny the danger. It is spoken because of who stands beside you in the danger, the God who promises his presence on the very ground that frightens you most.
cultural: Joshua was told to be strong and courageous as he faced armies and an unknown land with Moses newly dead. The fishermen Jesus called knew the terror of a storm on the Sea of Galilee, and the early church heard fear not as you will be spared but as I am with you when you are not. Courage in the Bible is never the absence of fear.
historical: The martyrs of the early church walked toward death singing, not because they felt no fear but because they trusted a presence stronger than it. Across the centuries, from Polycarp in the second century to Dietrich Bonhoeffer facing the gallows in 1945, believers have located courage not in their own nerve but in the God who does not abandon his people.
application: Name the fear plainly rather than letting it run unspoken in the dark. Take the next faithful step even while afraid, since courage is fear that has prayed and moved anyway. Surround yourself with people who steady you. And anchor your mind on the promise of God's presence rather than on the size of the threat, returning to it as often as the fear returns.

verses.text: Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”
Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My right hand of righteousness.
Of David. The LORD is my light and my salvation— whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life— whom shall I dread?
For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
When I am afraid, I put my trust in You.

label: When You Are Trapped by Addiction
framing: Scripture is honest about the chains we cannot break ourselves, naming the misery of doing the very thing we hate. It does not offer willpower as the cure but a freedom that comes from outside us, and it insists that the one in bondage is not beyond reach.
cultural: Paul wrote of the war within, willing the good but doing the evil, to a world that knew slavery as a literal condition and used it as the picture for sin's grip. His readers understood being owned by a master you could not escape on your own, which is exactly the language Scripture uses for the hold of sin on the body and will.
historical: The church has long known that some chains require more than resolve. The recovery movement of the twentieth century, rooted in Christian conviction through the Oxford Group, built the Twelve Steps on confession, surrender to a higher power, and honest community, recovering an ancient truth that no one is freed alone and that grace meets us at the bottom.
application: Tell the truth to at least one safe person today, because addiction lives in secrecy and dies in the light. Get real help, a counselor, a recovery group, a medical professional, or a treatment program, and understand that needing them is not weakness but wisdom. Expect setbacks without surrendering to them. If you or someone you love is in crisis, in the US call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and for substance help call SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357.

verses.text: I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out. For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.

No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.
So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.
But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me.
Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.

label: When You Are Seriously Ill
framing: Scripture does not promise that the faithful are spared sickness, and it refuses to read illness as a verdict on your worth. It gives you a God near to the brokenhearted, permission to ask boldly for healing, and the deeper assurance that nothing in your body can separate you from his love.
cultural: In the ancient world illness often meant exclusion, the leper put outside the camp, the sick assumed to be under judgment. Into that, Jesus touched the untouchable and ate with the unclean, and the Psalms gave the sick a language to cry out from the bed of affliction without pretending to feel fine. Sickness was not hidden; it was prayed.
historical: The church built hospitals because it believed the sick body mattered to God. Basil of Caesarea opened a great house of care in the fourth century, and across history believers have held together two things our world separates, the work of medicine and the work of prayer, treating the doctor's hands as one of the means by which God heals.
application: Use every good gift God provides, the doctor, the treatment, the medicine, as part of his care rather than apart from it. Let people pray over you and carry you when you cannot carry yourself. Tell God the truth about your fear and your pain. And as illness deepens, talk openly with your medical team, a counselor, or hospice care about what you face, since walking toward honest help is itself an act of faith.

verses.text: The LORD will sustain him on his bed of illness and restore him from his bed of sickness.

Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.
My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.

label: When God Feels Far Away
framing: There are seasons when prayer feels like talking to the ceiling and the old joy has gone cold. Scripture treats this not as proof of God's absence but as a known country of the faithful, where God is often nearest when he feels furthest, doing work below the level of feeling.
cultural: The Psalmist cried out, How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever, and was not corrected for it. Israel knew literal wilderness, forty years of barren ground where God fed them daily but the manna grew tiresome. The biblical writers gave us a vocabulary for the dry season precisely because they lived through it and refused to fake their way past it.
historical: The church has named this experience for centuries. John of the Cross, in the sixteenth century, called it the dark night of the soul and insisted it was God's purifying work rather than his withdrawal. Mother Teresa lived decades in such dryness while serving faithfully, proof that the dry heart and the obedient life can run side by side.
application: Keep to the practices, prayer, Scripture, worship, when the feeling is gone, because faith is not built on the feeling and often returns through the habit. Tell God honestly that he feels distant rather than performing a closeness you do not feel. Let others pray when you cannot. And if the dryness is a heaviness that will not lift, talk with a pastor or counselor, since dryness and depression can wear the same face.

verses.text: For the choirmaster. A Maskil of the sons of Korah. As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?
For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?

When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze.
The LORD Himself goes before you; He will be with you. He will never leave you nor forsake you. Do not be afraid or discouraged.”
A Psalm of David, when he was in the Wilderness of Judah. O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water.

label: When You Have Lost Hope
framing: Scripture meets despair without flinching and without scolding. It records God's own people praying that they would rather die, and it answers not with a rebuke but with food, rest, and presence. Your life is not yours to throw away, and the darkness you are in is not the final word over you.
cultural: Elijah, just after his greatest victory, collapsed under a tree and begged God to take his life. Job cursed the day he was born. The Psalmist said darkness was his only friend. The biblical world made room for words this honest because it knew despair was real, and it never treated the suicidal cry as a sin to be hushed but as a soul to be reached.
historical: The church has not always handled despair well, sometimes adding shame to it, but its better tradition has insisted that the despairing are precious and never beyond rescue. Charles Spurgeon, the most famous preacher of the nineteenth century, spoke openly of being so low he wished he had never been born, and used his own darkness to reach others in theirs.
application: If you are thinking of ending your life, please reach out right now. In the US, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, available day and night, or go to your nearest emergency room. Tell one real person today, do not carry this alone, and let a doctor or counselor in. Hold on through this hour, then the next. The darkness is real, but it is not the truth about you, and it does not get the last word.

verses.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.

while he himself traveled on a day’s journey into the wilderness. He sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die. “I have had enough, LORD,” he said. “Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.” Then he lay down under the broom tree and fell asleep. Suddenly an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat.”
Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.
We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.
Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!

label: When You Are Facing Death
framing: Scripture does not pretend death is nothing. It calls death an enemy, the last one. But it announces over that enemy a stranger thing still, that Christ has gone through death ahead of you and come out the other side, so that for those who are his the grave is a passage and not a wall.
cultural: The ancient world feared death as a shadowy nothing, and even Israel long spoke of the grave as silence. Into that, the resurrection of Jesus landed as scandal and shock, an empty tomb that rewrote what death could mean. The early Christians faced execution with a calm that baffled Rome, because they were sure of a life on the far side of dying.
historical: The church developed an entire art of dying well, the ars moriendi of the late medieval period, teaching believers to face the end with honesty and hope rather than terror. From the martyrs who sang at the stake to the modern hospice movement, founded by the Christian physician Cicely Saunders in 1967, the church has insisted that the dying be accompanied, not abandoned.
application: Speak openly about what you face, with God and with the people you love, rather than facing it alone behind a brave mask. Put your affairs and your relationships in order, say the words that need saying, and make peace where you can. Lean on hospice and palliative care, your medical team, and a pastor, for the dying deserve comfort and company. And rest your hope not in your own strength but in the One who has already passed through death for you.

verses.text: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?”
Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.
“Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?”
We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
